messages.subject: Re: two observers, one of them measured in whole numbers
parts:
Hi Sacha,
(adding to Eric's comment)

Thanks for the feedback (off list), where you mention that distances are=20
up to 20 meters, with esw between 15 and 20. So you are in between the=20
numbers Eric mentioned. Still...

I would really not implement your adding error suggestion. You know what=20
error you add, but you don't know what error you end up, because the=20
observations you add error to already have unknown error. So you're not=20
really getting any closer to truth, you just have numbers that to some=20
extent look less suspicious to a human eye. In practice, for the=20
fitting, things won't change much, and yet you have another convoluted=20
and not easy to justify process to explain in your methods section.

I would rather use truncation points which were something like=20
0,1.5,2.5,3.5,... presumably if the error is just in rounding to=20
integers, that means you end up with the observations in the right bin.

But to some extent I wonder if it will make much difference. Fitting is=20
often quite insensitive to moderate heaping, and you don't seem to have=20
an extreme version of heaping any way. With distances up to 20 meters,=20
if you had rounding to multiples of 5, you'd be in real trouble though.

It is very often that you don't get integer resolution, because=20
distances were "guesstimated", or that you do have higher resolution=20
than that, but it is meaningless. E.g. x's obtained by r sin theta, i.e.=20
perpendicular distances from radial distances and angles, seems to have=20
a precision that neither the original angles nor distances had, because=20
of the trigonometry function involved.

Cheers,

T.


On 07/12/2010 10:12, Sacha Viquerat wrote:
> > dear mailing list!
> > i've encountered the following problem:
> > in order to prepare a publication on animal densities, a two observer
> > survey had been conducted in 2009. we were now trying to pool the
> > observations BUT... one of the observers measured distance in integers,
> > therefore I assume this dataset to be somewhat rounded. is there a way
> > to cope with that? i was thinking of adding generated random numbers to
> > each sample, constructed in a way that they will not alter median, mean=
,
> > sd, and variance of the samples, though I am quite sure this would not
> > be appropriate.
